initial_prompt: Tell me more about the Calvin cycle

messages.content: Tell me more about the Calvin cycle

The Calvin cycle is the "synthesis" part of photosynthesis - where plants actually build sugar molecules from CO2.

It happens in three phases: First, the enzyme RuBisCO fixes CO2 onto a 5-carbon molecule (RuBP), creating two 3-carbon molecules. Second, those get reduced using energy from ATP and NADPH (made in the light reactions) into G3P - simple sugars. Third, most of the G3P regenerates RuBP to keep the cycle going, while some exits to become glucose.

The key insight is that it takes six turns of the cycle (fixing 6 CO2) to make one glucose molecule. It's called a "dark reaction" not because it happens at night, but because it doesn't directly need light - though it depends on products from the light reactions.

RuBisCO is worth noting - it's probably the most abundant enzyme on Earth, but it's remarkably slow and sometimes grabs O2 instead of CO2 (photorespiration), which is wasteful. Plants like corn have evolved C4 pathways partly to work around RuBisCO's limitations.
